etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English closet, from Old French closet, from clos (“private space”) +‎ -et (diminutive suffix), from Latin clausum. Equivalent to close +‎ -et, but generally applied in French solely to small open-air enclosures.

definitions.definition: A small room within a house used to store clothing, food, or other household supplies.

quote.text: A Closet full of shelves... it... should therefore be called a Cupboard rather than a Closet.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Any private space, (particularly) bowers in the open air.

quote.text: A slepe hym toke / In hys closet.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A private room used by women to groom and dress themselves.

quote.text: Closet for a lady to make her redy in, chamberette.

definitions.definition: (archaic) A private room used for prayer or other devotions.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Matthew 6:6:
quote.text: When thou prayest, enter into thy closet.

definitions.definition: (figuratively, archaic) A place of (usually, fanciful) contemplation and theorizing.

quote.citation: 1594–1597, Richard Hooker, chapter 24, in J[ohn] S[penser], editor, Of the Lawes of Ecclesiastical Politie, […], London:  […]  Will[iam] Stansby [for Matthew Lownes], published 1611, →OCLC, (please specify the page):
quote.text: [A]broad and at home, at their Tables or in their Closets  […]

definitions.definition: (archaic) The private residence or private council chamber of a monarch.
(now rare) Any private or inner room, (particularly):

quote.citation: 1765, [Oliver] Goldsmith, The Haunch of Venison, a Poetical Epistle to Lord Clare, Dublin:  […]  W. Whitestone, […], published 1776, →OCLC, page 9:
quote.text: VVhen come to the place vvhere vve all vvere to dine, / (A chair-lumber'd Cloſet, juſt tvvelve feet by nine) / My friend bid me vvelcome, but ſtruck me quite dumb / VVith tidings that Johnson and Burke coud not come:  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A pew or side-chapel reserved for a monarch or other feudal lord.

quote.citation: c. 1390, Sir Gawain & the Green Knight, §I, 934 ff.:
quote.text: Chaplayneȝ to þe chapeles chosen þe gate... / Þe lorde loutes þerto, & þe lady als, / In-to a comly closet coyntly ho entreȝ.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) One used to store valuables.

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii], line 130:
quote.text: But heere's a Parchment... I found it in his Closset, 'tis his Will.

definitions.definition: (archaic) One used to store curiosities.

quote.text: Mr. Tradescant and his wife told me they had been long considering upon whom to bestow their closet of curiosities when they died.

quote.citation: 1681, Marquis of Halifax, Seasonable Addresses to the Houses of Parliament in Concise Succession, page 10:
quote.text: The late House of Commons have... seiz'd Closets and Writings without Information.

definitions.definition: (figuratively) A secret or hiding place, (particularly) the hiding place in English idioms such as in the closet and skeleton in the closet.

quote.citation: 1530, chapter II, in Myroure of Oure Ladye, page 233:
quote.text: Went the sonne of god oute of the pryuy closet of the maydens wombe.

definitions.definition: (slang, uncommon) Clipping of closet case.
A private cabinet, (particularly):
(US, Philippines) One intended for storing clothes or bedclothes.
(obsolete) Clipping of closet of ease, (later, UK) clipping of water closet: a room containing a toilet.
(now chiefly Scotland, Ireland) Any small room or side room.
(heraldry) An ordinary similar to a bar but half as broad.

quote.text: A Closset is the halfe of the Barre, and tenne of them maie be borne in one fielde.

definitions.definition: (Scotland, obsolete) A sewer.
The state of having one's sexual orientation a secret.

quote.citation: 1985 August 24, Michael Bronski, “Rock Hudson: The Great Gay Hope”, in Gay Community News, volume 13, number 7, page 15:
quote.text: 6 o'clock TV news specials concerning a famous Hollywood movie star who has been diagnosed with [AIDS]. It had to happen sooner or later. (In fact it probably has happened sooner, but the tenor of the times and the closets of the people were no doubt more secure.)

definitions.definition: A state or condition of secrecy, privacy, or obscurity.
(archaic) A compendium of knowledge, possibly from closet as a room?
(obsolete) Private.
Closeted, secret (especially with reference to gay people who are in the closet).

quote.citation: 1940, Walton Hall Smith with Ferdinand Christian Helwig, Liquor, the servant of man:
quote.text: I wonder if there is another in the world that could produce, among perfectly normal people, this strangest quirk in the agenda of liquordom, the closet drinker.

definitions.definition: Denoting anything kept a secret or private.
(transitive) To shut away for private discussion.
(transitive) To put into a private place for a secret interview or interrogation.

quote.citation: 1834–1874, George Bancroft, History of the United States, from the Discovery of the American Continent, volume (please specify |volume=I to X), Boston, Mass.: Little, Brown and Company [et al.], →OCLC:
quote.text: He was to call a new legislature, to closet its members.

quote.citation: 1856–1870, James Anthony Froude, History of England from the Fall of Wolsey to the Death of Elizabeth, volume (please specify |volume=I to XII), London: Longmans, Green, and Co., →OCLC:
quote.text: He had been closeted with De Quadra.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To shut up in, or as in, a closet for concealment or confinement.

quote.citation: 1784, William Cowper, Tirocinium, or A Review of Schools‎[1]:
quote.text: See what contempt is fallen on human kind;  […]  See Bedlam's closeted and handcuff'd charge / Surpass'd in frenzy by the mad at large;

[…]  she had to look twice over her shoulder when the Gay Northeasters and the City Belles strolled down Seventh Avenue, they were so handsome. But this envy-streaked pleasure Alice closeted, and never let the girl see how she admired those ready-for-bed-in-the-street clothes.
